name: Hardy–Weinberg from the Heterozygote Frequency
seoTitle: Hardy–Weinberg from the Heterozygote Frequency Calculator
seoDesc: Heterozygote frequency 2pq is a quadratic in q, so it has two solutions — a fact that bites anyone converting a carrier rate back into an allele frequency. Fr
summary:
Heterozygote frequency 2pq is a quadratic in q, so it has two solutions — a fact that bites anyone converting a carrier rate back into an allele frequency. It returns q (lower root), q (upper root), p for the lower root and homozygote frequency, lower root, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator solves both branches and reports which one applies to your population. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hardy–Weinberg from the Heterozygote Frequency
sections.html:
2q² − 2q + h = 0, so q = [1 ± √(1 − 2h)] ÷ 2

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
hobserved heterozygote frequency0–0.5
qrecessive allele frequency0–1
1 − 2hthe discriminant; negative means no solution—

sections.title: How do I use the Hardy–Weinberg from the Heterozygote Frequency?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: heterozygote frequency (2pq) of 0.42.

Substituting them into the formula gives q (lower root) of 0.3, q (upper root) of 0.7, p for the lower root of 0.7, homozygote frequency, lower root of 0.58, maximum possible 2pq of 0.5.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• 2pq never exceeds 0.5, so a reported heterozygote frequency above 50% cannot come from a two-allele locus at equilibrium — check the data before trusting the roots.

  • The two roots are mirror images: q and 1 − q give the same heterozygote frequency, so the data alone cannot tell you which allele is common.

  • Real populations often have fewer heterozygotes than 2pq predicts (a Wahlund effect from population structure), which is one reason the observed value may be the more useful input.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Entering 42 for 42% instead of 0.42.
  • Taking the lower root without checking which allele is the rare one.
  • Using this inversion when the locus has more than two alleles.

faq.q: What does the Hardy–Weinberg from the Heterozygote Frequency actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns q (lower root), q (upper root), p for the lower root and homozygote frequency, lower root. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
